lens: facts and integrity: every quotation, number, date, name, title and attribution in the published JSON checked against the claims ledger (livewell-land/docs/work/essays/ledgers/the-children-rome-threw-away.md), the ESV copy (mdbible json/ESV.json, commit fd66568), the BSB chapter files, primary texts re-read today (ANF Justin and Tertullian in scripts/data/history-sources/texts; Lake's Didache and Diognetus fetched again from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit; Fyfe's Tacitus, GITenberg 16927; NPNF Augustine Letter 98, Writings-Database 328918a; APIS translation and HGV metadata for P.Oxy. 744, idp.data 1124e40), and 16 web searches

findings.where: ## What the First Christians Taught, second paragraph (Diognetus): "Then he names what sets them apart, and the first thing he names concerns their children:"
findings.problem: (c) The essay says something the text does not support, and the ledger's own wording differs. Lake's Diognetus (Perseus, re-read today) puts 5.5 between the essay's paraphrase of 5.4 (Greek and barbarian cities, local customs in clothing and food) and the quotation from 5.6. Section 5.5 already names what sets Christians apart: "They dwell in their own fatherlands, but as if sojourners in them; they share all things as citizens, and suffer all things as strangers. Every foreign country is their fatherland, and every fatherland is a foreign country." So the first thing he names is not about children. Ledger line 22 makes the narrower claim, "5.6 is the first household practice named". The essay widened it to "the first thing he names".
findings.fix: Replace "and the first thing he names concerns their children:" with "and the first custom he names concerns their children:". The rest of the sentence and the quotation stay as they are.

findings.where: ## Did the Early Christians Rescue Abandoned Babies?, second paragraph: "In 442 a council of bishops at Vaison, in Gaul, made provision for infants left at churches."
findings.problem: (b)/(c) The specific claim "infants left at churches" rests only on a popular summary. Ledger line 60 cites an Italian article (Vaison 442, canons 9 and 10) and Aleteia ("an abandoned child to find sanctuary in a church"). Today's three searches found the same two sources. The scholarly one (revistas.ucm.es) says only that canons 9 and 10 deal with abandoned infants. The Aleteia line is the only support for "left at churches", and nobody has seen the canon text. The date, the place and the subject are all verified.
findings.fix: Generalize to what the scholarly source supports: "In 442 a council of bishops at Vaison, in Gaul, made rules about abandoned infants." Or keep the sentence as it is only if a later run reads canons 9 and 10 of Vaison (Concilia Galliae, or Hefele) and finds that they speak of infants left at a church.

findings.where: ## Why Christians Saw Children Differently, second paragraph: "When people brought them to him and the disciples tried to send them away, Mark says Jesus \"was indignant\""
findings.problem: (a)/(e) This paraphrase of Mark 10:13 has no ledger line. The ESV reads "the disciples rebuked them", and the BSB reads "the disciples rebuked those who brought them". Neither says they tried to send the children away. That reading is fair but goes past the verse. The quotations from 10:14 and 10:16 that follow are exact.
findings.fix: Replace "and the disciples tried to send them away" with "and the disciples rebuked them", then add a ledger line for Mark 10:13 (ESV copy).

findings.where: ## Did the Early Christians Rescue Abandoned Babies?, first and last paragraphs: "they said so publicly, to emperors and to the crowds that accused them" and "It said so to emperors who could have its members killed."
findings.problem: (a) No ledger line supports the plural "emperors". Of the works quoted, only Justin addresses an emperor. Tertullian's Apology addresses Roman magistrates. The plural does hold: the ANF Chapter I of the First Apology (re-read today in scripts/data/history-sources/texts/justin-first-apology.html) is addressed "To the Emperor Titus Aelius Adrianus Antoninus Pius Augustus Caesar, and to his son Verissimus the Philosopher, and to Lucius the Philosopher", that is, to the emperor and to the two heirs who later reigned as Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus.
findings.fix: No change to the essay. Add a ledger line that cites the ANF Chapter I address as support for "emperors".

findings.where: ## A Letter from Alexandria, third paragraph ("He is a working man far from home") and ## Why Roman Families Left Children Outside, first paragraph ("A laborer's household lived close to the edge")
findings.problem: (c) Ledger line 10 calls Hilarion "probably a laborer" on the strength of Caragounis. But the HGV metadata the ledger itself cites (idp.data HGV_meta_EpiDoc/HGV21/20442.xml, re-read today) lists the keyword "Soldat" (soldier), so his trade is disputed. The essay is safe as written: "working man" fits either reading, and the laborer sentence is a general statement about households.
findings.fix: No change to the essay. Do not sharpen "working man" to "laborer" in any later pass. Add to ledger line 10: "HGV keyword 'Soldat'; occupation disputed; essay says only 'working man'."

findings.where: Ledger, "Original wording, for restoring", aging-out bullet (essay sentence: "More than fifteen thousand young people aged out of foster care in 2025 without a permanent family, by the National Council for Adoption's count.")
findings.problem: (c) The ledger says the writer's original "2023 ... by the National Council for Adoption's count" would misattribute the figure. Today's search summary of adoptioncouncil.org reports that NCFA's own previous fact sheet gave 15,590 youth who aged out without a permanent family in FY23, which is the writer's original figure. So the original was an NCFA count after all. The essay's current sentence is also verified: the same summary reports NCFA's 2026 page with 15,030 for 2025, reported on the federal fiscal year, with FY24 data missing Washington.
findings.fix: No change to the essay: the 2025 figure is newer, so do not restore 2023. Correct the ledger bullet to say that NCFA's 2025 fact sheet gave 15,590 for FY23, so the original was not a misattribution, only older.

clean_checks: Non-Scripture quotations, all verbatim against texts re-read today: Hilarion (APIS translation in idp.data Translations/20/20442-2.xml: "if you bear a child and it is male, let it be; if it is female, cast it out."); Didache 2.2 and Diognetus 5.6 (Lake, Perseus XML fetched again; both files name Lake as translator); Justin, First Apology 27 (two quotations) and 29 (ANF repo text, chapter headings confirmed); Tertullian, Apology 9 (three quotations, all between the Chapter IX and Chapter X headings; the baby-eating charge is in Chapter VII); Tacitus, Histories 5.5 (Fyfe, GITenberg 16927-8.txt lines 11861 to 11862); Augustine, Letter 98.6 (NPNF, headed "LETTER XCVIII. (A.D. 408.)"); Harris (the JRS 1994 abstract in today's search reads "very often but by no means always resulting in death,").

Quotation punctuation: the only differences are at the end of quotations, where American usage puts a period or comma inside the marks. Justin's ";" became "." and his "prostitution." became "prostitution,"; Augustine's "passer-by," became "passer-by."; Exodus 2:6 gained a comma; Tacitus's capital was lowered (the ledger records this). No word inside any quotation differs from its source.

Scripture: all 19 quoted passages match the local ESV copy word for word, checked by script: Genesis 1:27; Mark 10:14 (two) and 10:16; Matthew 18:5, 18:6 and 2:18; Ezekiel 16:5 and 16:6 (twice); Exodus 1:22 and 2:6; Galatians 4:5; Psalm 68:5-6 (body and Closing Texts); James 1:27; Romans 8:1; Psalm 34:18; Psalm 27:10. LORD is kept as in the printed ESV. Each reference was also checked for sense against the BSB chapter files, and every verse says what the essay uses it for (Ezekiel 16:4-6 is the exposed infant, Exodus 2:3-6 the basket and Pharaoh's daughter, Matthew 2:16-18 Herod and Jeremiah). Paraphrases sit outside quotation marks (Matthew 18:2 and 18:6, James 1:27 "pure before God the Father").
Exclamation points appear only inside quoted Ezekiel 16:6, both times with the reference. No em-dashes. One semicolon outside quotations (the Datheus sentence), as the ledger says.

Dates: 1 BC (HGV origDate 17 June 1 BC); 408 (NPNF heading); "four centuries after Hilarion" and "nearly a century after Constantine's conversion" (312 to 408) both hold; 331, 374, 442, 787 (archpriest Datheus, restored in correction 15), Tertullian 197, Justin "in the 150s", Tacitus early second century, Diognetus "probably" second century, Texas 1999, January 2021, Tuam 1925 to 1961, Bethany 1922 to 1949 and 2010, Fessler 1945 to 1973, 30 September 2024. Each matches its ledger line.

Numbers: more than 325,000 in foster care (today's search: 328,947 preliminary, revised to 327,364 in ACF's FY 2025 release; both clear the bar); more than fifteen thousand aged out in 2025 (today's search: NCFA, 15,030); Ireland 18 institutions (14 plus 4), about 56,000 mothers, 57,000 children, about 9,000 deaths, 15 percent; Tuam 796; Bethany more than two hundred (219); Fessler about 1.5 million; Boswell 20 to 40 percent of children in the first three centuries (today's search: encyclopedia.com); Kertzer hundreds of thousands. All match the ledger.

Names and titles: Hilarion, Alis, Aphrodisias, P.Oxy. 744, Oxyrhynchus; Kirsopp Lake; Justin and Antoninus Pius; Tertullian at Carthage; Tacitus; Augustine; Datheus; Valentinian I; Constantine; John Boswell, The Kindness of Strangers; W. V. Harris; Donald Engels; Rodney Stark; David Kertzer, Sacrificed for Honor; Catherine Corless; the Bon Secours Sisters; Bethany Home and Mount Jerome; Ann Fessler, The Girls Who Went Away; the Baby Moses law. All are on their ledger lines. The Canada affiliations were confirmed again today (Andrews and the Anglican Journal: most of the 60 to 80 homes were Catholic or Salvation Army, a few Anglican or United). The Kertzer "laws" claim was confirmed again in the publisher's description and the reviews. The book text itself was not seen, and the ledger says so.

Every ledger correction (1 to 17) and every voice-pass change that touches a claim is in the published text word for word, including "Few people around him would have expected him to", "lived by a rule that would not let them put a child out at all", "written at Carthage around 197", "Most of those children" and "children who cannot stay with their own families". The JSON body is identical to docs/work/essays/the-children-rome-threw-away.md apart from a trailing newline.

Living people (f): Corless, Kertzer, Fessler, Harris and Engels are each described only by the work the ledger verifies, and nothing unfair is said about any of them. The Bon Secours Sisters, the Salvation Army and the churches named are described as the sources describe them. Bethany is attributed to the people who ran it, not to a church, matching the caveat in ledger line 83.

Links: /writing/the-conservative-blind-spot and /writing/the-progressive-blind-spot are live on the shelf. /writing/the-early-church-under-rome is pending, with its rewrite in client/public/essays/, so it will be public. /help is linked, and the 988 line is the wording the brief prescribes.

Restorations (g), none proposed. Hilarion's original "if it is a male, let it live; if it is a female, expose it.": a search summary said the Diotima page renders the verbs "let it live" and "expose it", but no source seen printed the full sentence, an exact-phrase search found nothing, and diotima-doctafemina.org is blocked here (the proxy refused it and WebFetch could not resolve it). The original stays unrestored and the verified APIS text stays. The "sister could mean a wife" clause: no new source seen. Foster care "about 329,000 ... preliminary": superseded by the revised 327,364, so not restored. Aging out "2023": confirmed as an NCFA FY23 count (15,590) but older than the essay's 2025 figure, so not restored (see the last finding). Datheus "archpriest" is already restored.
